beats.title: Lesson 5 — Brute-forcing the OpenPLC Login
beats.sub: Weak credentials are the front door
beats.say: Welcome back to CybICS. Not every way into a controller is a protocol trick. Often it is the front door: a weak password on the web interface. In this lesson we brute-force the OpenP L C login.

beats.head: No lockout, weak passwords
beats.body:
OpenPLC's web interface is a classic form login. It has no rate-limiting and no lockout, so an attacker can try passwords as fast as the server answers.
  • We target the admin account with a dictionary attack.
  • The tool ffuf tries each word and filters out the fixed-size wrong-login page, so the correct password stands out.
  • Maps to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS T0812 Default Credentials and T0859 Valid Accounts.
beats.say: OpenP L C's web interface is a classic form login, and it has no rate limiting and no lockout. So an attacker can try passwords as fast as the server answers. We target the admin account with a dictionary attack. The tool ffuf tries each word from a list and filters out the fixed size wrong login page, so the one correct password stands out immediately. This maps to MITRE default credentials and valid accounts.

beats.caption: Brute-force the admin password with ffuf
beats.say: We point ffuf at the login with the classic rockyou wordlist. Thousands of guesses a second stream at the server. And within a second, one word gets a different response, a redirect instead of the login page: ramirez. That is the admin password.

beats.head: From a password to the plant
beats.body:
The OpenPLC web UI is not just a status page — it can upload and start control logic. Admin access here means an attacker can reprogram the PLC.

First, we use the cracked password to log in and read the challenge flag straight from the account page.
beats.say: This password is not a trophy on its own. The OpenP L C web interface can upload and start control logic, so admin access here means an attacker can reprogram the P L C itself. To prove the access, we use the cracked password to log in and read the challenge flag straight from the account page.

beats.caption: Log in with the cracked password and read the flag
beats.cmd: curl -s -c /tmp/oc -b /tmp/oc -X POST -d 'username=admin&password=ramirez' http://172.18.0.3:8080/login -o /dev/null; curl -s -c /tmp/oc -b /tmp/oc http://172.18.0.3:8080/users | grep -oiE 'CybICS\([^)]*\)'
beats.say: We log in over the command line with the cracked credentials, and pull the users page. There is the flag, sitting in the admin account: CybICS, zero p e n P L C. Valid credentials gave us everything a legitimate operator can see.

beats.caption: Submit the flag in the CybICS dashboard - on the attack machine
beats.say: We complete the challenge on the dashboard, opening the OpenP L C password attack and submitting the flag we recovered from the account.

beats.head: What we learned
beats.body:
• A weak password on a control-system web UI is a direct path to the process.
  • No lockout means brute force is cheap.
  • Defences: strong, unique passwords, account lockout and multi-factor, and keep the interface off any reachable network.
beats.say: To recap: a weak password on a control system web interface is a direct path to the process, and without a lockout, brute force is cheap. The defences are the ordinary ones that ICS so often skips: strong unique passwords, account lockout, multi factor authentication, and keeping the interface off any network an attacker can reach.

beats.title: Flag captured: CybICS(0penPLC)
beats.sub: Next lesson: overwriting a process value  ·  github.com/mniedermaier/CybICS
beats.say: Flag captured. With credentials in hand, the next lessons put that access to work against the process itself.
